1→# Architecture
   2→
   3→This document explains the system to someone who has read the README and has five minutes.
   4→Every claim here describes the code as it stands; nothing is planned or partial except where
   5→the Limits section says so plainly.
   6→
   7→## Overview
   8→
   9→Ryde is a multi-agent dispute resolution system for ride-hailing: a party files a dispute
  10→through a web intake form, and the system resolves the two categories it handles — route
  11→deviation and no-show charge — end to end. Three agents do the work: a Rider Advocate and a
  12→Driver Advocate each build their side's case from the evidence, and a Judge weighs both
  13→cases, applies company policy and issues a ruling with a confidence score. Every computed
  14→figure the agents argue from comes from a deterministic Evidence Pack calculated in Python
  15→before any model is called; agents cite pack fields by reference and are forbidden from
  16→doing their own arithmetic, and the only other number they see is the amount the party
  17→asked for. The decisions that must never depend on a model's obedience — the confidence
  18→threshold, the SGD 50 autonomous cap, the requirement that a route ruling rest on a measured
  19→deviation, the one-round follow-up limit, and the routing of out-of-scope categories to
  20→human review — are enforced in Python code, not asked of the model in a prompt. The system
  21→has two surfaces: an operator console that shows the full case file and the agent-to-agent
  22→traffic, and a party page where the filing party submits the form and reads only what they
  23→are allowed to read.
  24→
  25→## Diagram
  26→
  27→The whole system on one page. A dispute arrives either through the web intake form or the
  28→command-line runner; the two swappable inputs (the policy document and the dataset pack)
  29→enter from the side. Every step of a run lands in the event log, and the operator console
  30→renders the event strip embedded in the case file — opening each event's full payload from
  31→the run files the operator attaches.
  32→
  33→```mermaid
  34→flowchart TD
  35→    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> B["Server"]
  36→    PACK --> CL["Command-line runner"]
  37→    A["Rider intake form"] --> B
  38→    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
  39→    CL --> C
  40→    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
  41→    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
  42→    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
  43→    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
  44→    POL --> J["Judge"]
  45→    E --> RA
  46→    E --> DA
  47→    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
  48→    DA --> S
  49→    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
  50→    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
  51→    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
  52→    S -- "No" --> J
  53→    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
  54→    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
  55→    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
  56→    O2 -- "Candidate ruling queued" --> H
  57→    J -- "Model could not answer" --> H
  58→    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
  59→    J -.-> L
  60→    L -- "Embedded in the case file" --> K["Operator console"]
  61→```
  62→
  63→## Components
  64→
  65→| Component | File(s) | Responsibility |
  66→|---|---|---|
  67→| Pipeline | `app/pipeline.py` | Runs one dispute end to end, moves the case between agents, records every step |
  68→| Dispute record and routing | `app/dispute.py` | Parses the two record shapes, normalises categories, routes out-of-scope filings away |
  69→| Evidence layer | `app/evidence/compute.py` | Computes the Evidence Pack by plain arithmetic; a missing input inside a record becomes a null with a note, never a guess — but a route case with no trip record, or a no-show case with no cancellation record, aborts the run before any pack is built |
  70→| Agent scaffolding | `app/agents/base.py` | Shared prompts, the LLM call, and citation validation against the pack and the policy |
  71→| Rider Advocate | `app/agents/rider_advocate.py` | Argues the rider's side from the pack and the policy |
  72→| Driver Advocate | `app/agents/driver_advocate.py` | Argues the driver's side from the pack and the policy |
  73→| Judge | `app/agents/judge.py` | Weighs both cases, issues one ruling, withholds it behind the gates |
  74→| Event log | `app/events.py` | The append-only record of who said what to whom, with full payloads on disk |
  75→| Output contracts | `app/schemas.py` | The typed shapes agents must produce; builds the party-facing decision message |
  76→| Policy loader | `app/policy.py` | Reads the policy document, extracts rule IDs, fails loudly when it is missing |
  77→| Mock LLM | `app/llm/mock.py` | Deterministic stand-in provider; its free-text fields — claim summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation — carry a `MOCK` prefix, while actions, rule IDs and evidence refs do not |
  78→| Tencent adapter | `app/llm/tencent.py` | The real provider: calls one Tencent Cloud ADP app per agent over HTTP |
  79→| HTTP server | `app/server.py` | The intake API, the party view allowlist, and static files for both pages |
  80→| Command-line runner | `app/cli.py` | Runs one dispute from the terminal and prints the event strip |
  81→| Runtime configuration | `app/config.json` | Confidence threshold, autonomous cap, default dataset pack, provider settings |
  82→| Operator console | `ui/app.js` | Renders the case file: grievance, evidence, both claims, resolution, event strip |
  83→| Party page | `ui/party/party.js` | The intake form and the outcome view the filing party sees |
  84→| Policy document | `docs/policy.md` | The rule set the agents cite, with per-rule provenance |
  85→
  86→## Lifecycle of a dispute
  87→
  88→`run_dispute` in `app/pipeline.py` walks one dispute through these steps, in this order,
  89→emitting an event at each:
  90→
  91→1. `run.started` — the system records the dispute id, category, LLM provider, confidence
  92→   threshold and the policy rule IDs in force.
  93→2. `dispute.filed` — the raw intake-form submission is logged exactly as it arrived.
  94→3. **Routing.** If the category is outside the two handled ones, the run emits
  95→   `dispute.routed_to_human_review`, then `party.notified` with the neutral support message,
  96→   then `run.completed` — and no agent runs at all.
  97→4. `evidence.pack_built` — the Evidence Pack is computed in Python, before any LLM call,
  98→   and offered to the agents as the source of every computed figure — the only other
  99→   number they see is the amount the party claimed.
 100→5. `case.assigned` — once to each advocate.
 101→6. Each advocate runs and emits `advocate.case_submitted` to the Judge with its case. When
 102→   an advocate needs more from the filing party, it selects offered slot IDs and emits
 103→   `advocate.follow_up_requested` in the first round with both the selected slots and the
 104→   rendered questions. Code renders a bank sentence for a rider-filed dispute, or a form
 105→   sentence from an intake label for either filer; any question text written by the model
 106→   is ignored. The party-safety check remains a backstop, and only rendered questions that
 107→   pass it reach the party.
 108→7. **Stop and ask.** If there are questions to send and the dispute does not already carry
 109→   the party's answers, the run stops before the Judge: `party.notified` carries the
 110→   rendered questions — or, when none survive the backstop, plain template questions the
 111→   pipeline builds for blank intake fields — then `run.completed` records the `needs_info`
 112→   outcome. The party's answers start a fresh run, which is guaranteed to reach the Judge.
 113→8. `judge.deliberation_started` — both cases are handed to the Judge together.
 114→9. The Judge rules: `judge.ruling_issued` when every gate passes, or
 115→   `judge.ruling_withheld` when one fails — the candidate ruling is recorded either way.
 116→10. `party.notified` — the message the parties actually receive, as opposed to what was
 117→    decided internally.
 118→11. `run.completed` — the outcome is recorded and the case file is written.
 119→
 120→## The four outcomes
 121→
 122→| Outcome | When it happens | Did the Judge run? | Party page shows |
 123→|---|---|---|---|
 124→| `ruled` | The Judge issued a ruling and every gate passed | Yes | `decided` |
 125→| `withheld` | A gate stopped the ruling, or the model could not answer after its allowed retries | Yes for a gate — the candidate is recorded for a human reviewer, never delivered; no candidate exists for a model failure | `under_review` |
 126→| `human_review` | The category is outside the two the agents handle | No — routed away before any agent | `passed_to_support` |
 127→| `needs_info` | The advocates selected offered follow-up slots in the first round, or a blank form answer produced a template question | No — the run stops before the Judge | `needs_info` |
 128→
 129→## Gates enforced in code
 130→
 131→Six gates stand between a filing and a ruling, and each is enforced in Python, not asked of
 132→the model in a prompt:
 133→
 134→| Gate | File | Condition as written in code |
 135→|---|---|---|
 136→| Confidence threshold | `app/agents/judge.py` | `ruling.confidence < confidence_threshold` — the threshold is 0.65, read from `app/config.json` |
 137→| ESC-4, the autonomous cap | `app/agents/judge.py` | A money ruling whose `recommended_amount_sgd` exceeds the cap is withheld; the cap is SGD 50 from `app/config.json` |
 138→| ESC-2, unmeasured deviation | `app/agents/judge.py` | On a route-deviation case, `pack.route.deviation_pct is null` withholds the ruling — a route ruling must name the deviation it rests on |
 139→| One-round follow-up limit | `app/pipeline.py` | `if questions and not dispute.follow_up_answers` — a dispute is asked at most once; with answers present the Judge always runs and fresh questions are recorded but not sent |
 140→| Out-of-scope routing | `app/pipeline.py` | `if not dispute.is_agent_handled` — anything outside route deviation and no-show charge goes to human review before any agent runs; an unrecognised category normalises to "other" in `app/dispute.py` |
 141→| Answer once | `app/server.py` | The answers route claims the run with an exclusive create (`O_CREAT \| O_EXCL`) before re-running it — a `needs_info` run can be answered exactly once and cannot produce two rulings |
 142→
 143→Why in code? Because a prompt is a request — a model can misread it, and there is no
 144→recourse when it does. Code is a guarantee: the branch either runs or it does not, and the
 145→event log shows which. ESC-4 in particular moves money, so it must not depend on the LLM
 146→having read its instructions carefully.
 147→
 148→## Observability
 149→
 150→Every run writes three things under `runs/<run_id>/`:
 151→
 152→- `events.jsonl` — one JSON line per event, append-only, never rewritten: who sent what to
 153→  whom, when, with a one-line summary.
 154→- `payloads/` — the full payload behind each event, named by sequence number and event
 155→  type, so the strip stays readable and the detail stays one click away.
 156→- `case_file.json` — the assembled record: what was claimed, the evidence pack, both
 157→  advocate cases, the resolution, and the event strip. Self-contained, so one file tells
 158→  the whole story of one run.
 159→
 160→A run filed through the server writes one more file: `dispute.json`, the record the pipeline
 161→actually ran on (the command-line runner does not write it). When a `needs_info` run is
 162→answered, its directory also gains `answered.json`, recording which run the answers
 163→produced.
 164→
 165→The operator console (`ui/app.js`) renders the case file: the event strip shows one row per
 166→event — sequence, time, sender to recipient, summary — and expanding a row opens the full
 167→payload from the run directory attached in the browser. Payload references are sanitised, so
 168→a console loaded with a hostile file can be pointed at nothing outside the run. The
 169→command-line runner prints the same strip to the terminal.
 170→
 171→## What the parties see
 172→
 173→`party_view` in `app/server.py` is an allowlist that fails closed. The party page is handed
 174→exactly five keys — run id, dispute id, status, message, questions — and any malformed case
 175→file degrades to the neutral under-review message with no questions. A withheld ruling's
 176→amount and the Judge's confidence are structurally absent from everything the party is
 177→sent, not merely unrendered. `party_message_for_ruling` in `app/schemas.py` composes the
 178→decision message in code from structured fields — the action, the amount, and the plain
 179→titles of the policy rules cited — and the Judge's explanation never crosses this boundary:
 180→it stays in the operator console. Every non-decision status shows a canonical constant
 181→message, whatever a stale or planted case file might say. The two kinds of party-facing text
 182→are protected differently. The decision message is composed in code from structured fields,
 183→so nothing model-written reaches it: it names the action and the amount — a no-action ruling
 184→carries no amount — and at most three rule titles, never the escalation (ESC) rules. On a
 185→decided view the message leads with a demo notice whenever the ruling's LLM record does not
 186→prove the real provider — only a record that is a non-array dict whose provider field is
 187→exactly `tencent` suppresses it, and any other record, missing, mock or malformed, keeps it —
 188→so a decision made on an illustrative run never reads like a live review, while a proven
 189→real-provider decision shows no notice.
 190→Follow-up questions are selected by the advocates as slot IDs; code renders each sentence
 191→from the fixed category bank or from an intake form label. Bank slots are offered only when
 192→the rider filed, while form slots work for either filer. Any question text written by the
 193→model is ignored, so no model-written text reaches a party. The word check (`is_party_safe`,
 194→applied in `_questions_for_party` in `app/pipeline.py` and again in `party_view`) remains a
 195→backstop, as it is for the code-composed decision message. When no rendered question survives,
 196→the pipeline falls back to plain template questions built from the form's own labels. A run
 197→that asked for more information is answered through `POST /api/disputes/<run_id>/answers`, and
 198→the answers start a fresh run on the same dispute.
 199→
 200→## Policy and dataset packs
 201→
 202→`docs/policy.md` is data, not code: rules with IDs (GEN, EV, RD, NS, ESC families),
 203→preconditions written against pack fields in plain language, and per-rule provenance
 204→stating whether a rule comes from Ryde's own published policy, a comparable operator, or
 205→the project team. The pipeline reads it at the path in `app/config.json`; a different
 206→policy document drops in with no code change. Nothing in the code evaluates the
 207→preconditions — the Judge reads the rules and applies them in its reasoning. Citing a rule
 208→that does not exist is recorded rather than blocked: an unknown ID is logged under the
 209→ruling's `validation.unknown_rule_ids` with a note and the ruling still issues, but only
 210→titles of rules the policy actually defines can reach the party message.
 211→
 212→Two dataset packs live under `data/packs/`: `organiser-style-v1` — the default in
 213→`app/config.json` — which holds the corpus in the organisers' record shape, including their
 214→own DISP-002 verbatim; and `ryde-synth-v1`, the same 17 cases in this project's own record
 215→shape. Swapping corpora is a directory copy, never a code change. Each pack carries a
 216→`ground-truth.json` of expected outcomes, kept out of what the agents see: the agents get
 217→the dispute record, the evidence pack and the policy — never the answer — so replayed-run
 218→consistency can be measured honestly.
 219→
 220→## LLM provider
 221→
 222→Agent logic never talks to a vendor SDK. Every agent builds a request and calls one seam:
 223→the `LLMClient` interface in `app/llm/`, a single `complete` method whose response carries
 224→the text plus provenance (provider, model, usage, finish reason). Two adapters implement
 225→it. The mock provider, `app/llm/mock.py`, returns deterministic contract-shaped responses,
 226→so the full pipeline runs with no API key and the same dispute always produces the same
 227→decisions and the same computed figures (the run id and the event timestamps differ from
 228→run to run). Its free-text fields — claim summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation —
 229→carry a `MOCK` prefix, so a mock run can never be mistaken for a real ruling; actions, rule
 230→IDs and evidence refs are not prefixed. The party decision message, composed in code, is
 231→marked differently: on a decided party view it leads with a fixed demo notice stating that
 232→the decision came from an illustrative run and is not a live review, shown whenever the
 233→ruling's LLM record does not prove the Tencent provider, and only a record whose provider
 234→field is exactly `tencent` shows a decision with no notice. The Tencent adapter,
 235→`app/llm/tencent.py`, implements the same interface over Tencent Cloud ADP (Agent
 236→Development Platform). Each agent is its own published ADP app with its own key: Rider
 237→Advocate, Driver Advocate and Judge. The apps carry only a short role card; the adapter
 238→sends the full role prompt on every call, so the prompts live in this repo and every gate
 239→stays in Python. Three things about the endpoint shape the adapter. Tencent's web firewall
 240→blocks prompts that mix backticks with ASCII brackets, so the adapter drops backticks and
 241→sends full-width brackets, which the model reads the same way; a blocked call is classified
 242→as permanent and is never asked again. ADP reports errors inside a successful HTTP response,
 243→so the adapter reads every event rather than trusting the status code. The free plan allows
 244→10 calls a minute, so calls are spaced at least 6.5 seconds apart. The agent layer retries a
 245→transient failure up to three times, with waits of 2, 5 and 10 seconds; a contract failure
 246→is asked again once. A parsed reply is final: a low confidence or capped ruling is never
 247→asked again. One case shares a 120 seconds time budget from `llm.case_budget_seconds`; each
 248→retry is recorded as `llm.call_retried`. When the budget cannot cover a call or wait, or the
 249→model still cannot answer, the pipeline returns a withheld case and emits
 250→`dispute.escalated_on_model_failure`; the case file keeps the `model_failure` record for the
 251→reviewer. There is no silent fallback to the mock. The mock stays the default provider, so
 252→the tests and a fresh checkout need no keys; `--llm tencent` selects the real model.
 253→
 254→## Limits
 255→
 256→What the system does not do yet, stated plainly:
 257→
 258→- **A failed model call is escalated.** The party waits while retries run and sees the neutral
 259→  under-review message; after the case is queued for human review, the party is not notified later.
 260→- **Amounts must come back as JSON numbers.** A model reply carrying an amount as a string
 261→  is rejected, never converted, because the value moves money.
 262→- **Two categories only.** Route deviation and no-show charge. Property damage and safety
 263→  incidents route to human review by design.
 264→- **The driver-side form is not built.** The party page files as the rider only; the
 265→  pipeline itself accepts driver-filed disputes, but no web form offers it yet.
 266→- **Follow-up wording is code-owned.** Advocates select slot IDs; code renders each question
 267→  from the fixed category bank or an intake form label, and model-written question text is
 268→  ignored. Bank slots are rider-only; form slots are available to either filer.
 269→- **The word check is a backstop.** Rendered follow-up questions and the code-composed decision
 270→  message pass the keyword gate, which is not a semantic guarantee; blank fields still use
 271→  template questions built from the form's own labels.
 272→- **Policy preconditions are not evaluated by code.** The rules are written against pack
 273→  fields in plain language; nothing checks them mechanically, and the Judge applies them by
 274→  reading them.
 275→

1→# Dataset — labelled dispute corpus
   2→
   3→**Version 1.1 · two packs · 17 synthesised cases + the organisers' sample · generated 2026-09-21,
   4→organiser twins 2026-09-23 · policy version 1.0**
   5→
   6→The corpus the system is evaluated against. Like the policy, it is **data, not code**: the
   7→pipeline reads dispute records from a **dataset pack** under `data/packs/`, and a real dataset
   8→drops in with no code change.
   9→
  10→A pack is a directory with `disputes/` (one JSON file per case, named `<dispute_id>.json`),
  11→`ground-truth.json` (the labels) and `pack.json` (the manifest). `app/config.json` names the
  12→default pack; `--pack <name>` selects another for one CLI run.
  13→
  14→```
  15→data/packs/
  16→├── ryde-synth-v1/        our 17 synthesised cases, our record shape
  17→└── organiser-style-v1/   the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers' shape,
  18→                          plus the organisers' own DISP-002, verbatim
  19→```
  20→
  21→---
  22→
  23→## PROVENANCE — read this first
  24→
  25→**Every synthesised case in this corpus was authored by the project team. The one case that was
  26→not — the organisers' sample `DISP-002` — is reproduced byte-for-byte from the file they shared,
  27→and its provenance is theirs, not ours. No real trip, rider, driver, GPS trace or payment appears
  28→anywhere in either pack.**
  29→
  30→The challenge statement promised a sample dataset; one sample dispute (`DISP-002`) arrived on
  31→2026-09-23, which is a sample rather than a corpus, and Ryde publishes no dispute statistics —
  32→confirmed against LTA's Point-to-Point Quality of Service releases (which measure safety, not fare
  33→disputes), CASE's annual complaint reports (which have no ride-hailing category), and Ryde Group's
  34→own SEC filings. The absence is documented, not assumed.
  35→
  36→So the corpus is built rather than collected. Its **shapes** are grounded: the dispute patterns
  37→are modelled on publicly reported Singapore ride-hailing disputes (a driver marking arrival from
  38→the wrong location and letting the clock run; a fare adjusted after a destination change; a mass
  39→ERP mis-rating corrected on the regulator's direction), and the fee amounts and thresholds come
  40→from Ryde's published policy. The **data** is fabricated.
  41→
  42→**What this means for any number measured against it.** An accuracy figure from this corpus
  43→measures whether the system applies *our* policy to *our* cases consistently. It is a measure of
  44→internal consistency and calibration. It is **not** evidence of real-world accuracy, and must
  45→never be presented as one.
  46→
  47→---
  48→
  49→## The two packs
  50→
  51→**`ryde-synth-v1`** is the corpus described below: 17 synthesised cases in our own record shape,
  52→which is documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`.
  53→
  54→**`organiser-style-v1`** is the same 17 cases re-expressed in the shape of the organisers' sample
  55→(`dispute_ticket` / `trip_data` / `gps_telemetry` / `chat_logs` / `app_events`), plus `DISP-002`,
  56→the organisers' own no-show case, copied byte-for-byte from the file they shared and labelled from
  57→their stated ruling. Every synthetic case is a **twin** of its `ryde-synth-v1` counterpart: same
  58→facts, same numbers, different field names. `tests/test_organiser_pack.py` compares the two packs
  59→field by field, and `tests/test_organiser_reader.py` requires the Evidence Pack computed from a
  60→case and from its twin to agree on every number a ruling can rest on — a reader that maps one
  61→field wrong shows up there as a named mismatched field, not as a wrong ruling much later.
  62→
  63→Where the organisers' shape has no slot for something we carry (the claim amount, the intake-form
  64→answers, route-deviation trip fields), the case keeps it in a `ryde_extensions` block; `pack.json`
  65→lists exactly which fields those are. The reader maps the block back, so neither the Evidence Pack
  66→nor the agents need to know which pack a case came from.
  67→
  68→Each synthetic case also carries a top-level `cancellation_policy` stating the terms that govern
  69→it — Ryde's published 3-minute terms for our cases, the organisers' own 5 / 8 minute terms on
  70→their sample. That block reaches the agents as `cancellation.case_policy` on the Evidence Pack.
  71→
  72→## Layout
  73→
  74→```
  75→data/packs/<pack>/
  76→├── disputes/           one JSON file per case, named <dispute_id>.json
  77→├── ground-truth.json   the labels, deliberately kept out of the records
  78→└── pack.json           the manifest: name, format, case count, schema extensions
  79→```
  80→
  81→The labels live in a separate file on purpose. A label inside a dispute record would be visible
  82→to the agents through the intake or trip blocks, and every accuracy number measured against it
  83→would be worthless. `tests/test_corpus.py` enforces this: it scans each record for ground-truth
  84→keys and fails if one leaks.
  85→
  86→## The label shape
  87→
  88→```json
  89→{
  90→  "dispute_id": "RD-0101",
  91→  "category": "route_deviation",
  92→  "expected_outcome": "ruled",
  93→  "expected_action": "refund",
  94→  "expected_amount_sgd": 5.81,
  95→  "decisive_rule_ids": ["RD-1", "RD-2", "RD-3"],
  96→  "rationale": "50% / 3.2 km deviation clears both limbs of RD-1..."
  97→}
  98→```
  99→
 100→`expected_outcome` is one of `ruled`, `escalated`, `human_review`. `decisive_rule_ids` are the
 101→policy rules a correct ruling must rest on — a system that reaches the right answer by citing the
 102→wrong rule got there by luck, and the labels are built so that shows up.
 103→
 104→`rationale` exists so a human reviewer can disagree with a label. An unexplained label cannot be
 105→challenged, which makes it an assertion rather than ground truth.
 106→
 107→## Coverage
 108→
 109→| Cases | | |
 110→|---|---|---|
 111→| Route deviation | 9 | RD-0101 … RD-0109 |
 112→| No-show / cancellation fee | 7 | NS-0201 … NS-0207 |
 113→| Out of scope | 1 | OS-0301 |
 114→
 115→| Outcome | Cases |
 116→|---|---|
 117→| `ruled` → refund | 8 |
 118→| `ruled` → no action | 6 |
 119→| `escalated` | 2 |
 120→| `human_review` | 1 |
 121→
 122→**The balance is deliberate.** Roughly half the ruled cases find for the complainant and half do
 123→not. A corpus where every claim succeeds cannot demonstrate that the system is capable of saying
 124→no, and a dispute resolver that only ever refunds is not adjudicating — it is processing.
 125→`test_corpus.py` asserts both directions are present.
 126→
 127→Two cases escalate rather than resolve, for two different reasons: missing decisive evidence
 128→(RD-0108) and an amount above the autonomous cap (RD-0109). Escalation is a correct outcome under
 129→the policy, so it has to be in the corpus or the escalation path is untested. NS-0205 escalated
 130→until 2026-10-01; it now refunds under the rewritten NS-6 (a contested no-show with no recorded
 131→driver position is not a supported charge), and NS-6's conditions still send a riskier version of
 132→the same case to a human.
 133→
 134→## What each case is for
 135→
 136→**Route deviation**
 137→
 138→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 139→|---|---|---|
 140→| RD-0101 | Plain unjustified detour, both RD-1 limbs cleared | refund 5.81 |
 141→| RD-0102 | Material deviation the rider asked for (added stop) | no action |
 142→| RD-0103 | Deviation below both thresholds — routing judgement, not breach | no action |
 143→| RD-0104 | Long trip where the gross-km limb fires and the percentage barely does | refund 7.70 |
 144→| RD-0105 | Material unjustified deviation, but the rider paid the quoted fixed fare | no action |
 145→| RD-0106 | Fare breakdown does not reconcile — an overcharge with no deviation | refund 3.40 |
 146→| RD-0107 | Big duration overrun, negligible distance variance — traffic, not detour | no action |
 147→| RD-0108 | No estimated distance in the record, so materiality cannot be tested | escalate |
 148→| RD-0109 | Clear-cut deviation whose remedy exceeds the SGD 50 autonomous cap | escalate |
 149→
 150→RD-0109 is load-bearing beyond its label. It is the regression case for ESC-4: an adversarial
 151→review found the cap was stated in this document and in the labels but enforced **nowhere in
 152→code**, and a live run delivered "refund of SGD 55.16" straight to the parties at confidence 0.86.
 153→The cap is now a Python gate in `app/agents/judge.py` alongside the confidence gate, and
 154→`tests/test_gates.py` fails if it ever regresses.
 155→
 156→**No-show / cancellation fee**
 157→
 158→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 159→|---|---|---|
 160→| NS-0201 | Driver at pickup, waited 5.5 min — the fee was earned | no action |
 161→| NS-0202 | Driver at pickup but cancelled after 1.5 min, short of the minimum wait | refund 6.61 |
 162→| NS-0203 | Driver marked arrival 885 m away — the wait never started | refund 6.61 |
 163→| NS-0204 | Driver never arrived at all; rider charged for cancelling | refund 6.61 |
 164→| NS-0205 | Both sides assert opposite facts and no driver position was recorded: the fee has no GPS proof, so NS-6 refunds it (fee under SGD 10, clean rider record) | refund 6.61 |
 165→| NS-0206 | Cancellation inside the 3-minute free window | refund 6.61 |
 166→| NS-0207 | Waiting fee on a completed trip, driver at pickup | no action |
 167→
 168→**Out of scope**
 169→
 170→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 171→|---|---|---|
 172→| OS-0301 | A property-damage claim filed by a driver | human review, no agent ruling |
 173→
 174→RD-0103 carries a second purpose: its rider profile has a high dispute rate and a low trip count.
 175→The claim fails on RD-1's thresholds and **not** on the rider's history, which is what GEN-8
 176→requires. If a system starts declining claims because of who filed them, this is the case where
 177→that shows.
 178→
 179→## How it is generated
 180→
 181→`tools/build_corpus.py` writes both packs — `ryde-synth-v1` itself, and `organiser-style-v1` by
 182→transforming those records through `tools/organiser_pack.py` and copying in the organiser samples
 183→from `tools/organiser_samples/` as received. Both are **non-app tools**: nothing under `app/`
 184→imports from them.
 185→
 186→```bash
 187→python3 tools/build_corpus.py            # regenerate both packs into data/
 188→python3 tools/build_corpus.py --check    # fail if data/ differs from the generator
 189→```
 190→
 191→The generator exists because every case carries fare arithmetic and a GPS polyline that must agree
 192→with each other. Hand-written JSON drifts: a distance edited without recomputing the fare produces
 193→a record where the Evidence Pack calculates something different from what the case intends, and
 194→the label silently becomes a lie. Here the numbers derive from a handful of per-case parameters
 195→(actual km, quoted km, minutes, tariff), so they cannot come apart.
 196→
 197→**GPS traces are generated, not asserted.** Each route is a polyline walked along a bearing in
 198→equal legs, whose haversine length is the intended distance. The Evidence Pack then recomputes the
 199→distance from those points exactly as it would for a real trace — `test_corpus.py` asserts the
 200→pack never fell back to a stated distance. The traces are geometrically valid but they are not
 201→real Singapore roads; they start near Dhoby Ghaut and head northeast in a gentle zigzag.
 202→
 203→**Fares are computed with the pack's own formula**, `(base + per_km × km + per_min × min) × surge
 204→− promo`, and the breakdown components are the same terms with surge applied, so they sum to the
 205→charge. RD-0106 deliberately breaks that reconciliation by 3.40 — it is the only case where the
 206→breakdown is inconsistent, and that inconsistency is the thing being tested.
 207→
 208→## Verification
 209→
 210→`tests/test_corpus.py` (28 tests) is the guard on this artifact. It checks structure (every case
 211→labelled exactly once, no label leaking into a record, every label carrying a rationale), policy
 212→agreement (no label cites a rule that is not in `docs/policy.md`, and the thresholds the tests use
 213→are parsed from the policy's own parameters table rather than trusted as copies), and — the part
 214→that matters most — **evidence agreement**: every labelled refund amount must match a number the
 215→Evidence Pack actually computes from that record, and the policy's mechanical thresholds applied
 216→to the pack must not contradict the label.
 217→
 218→That last check earned its place during authoring. It caught two labels whose amounts were written
 219→by hand and were wrong: RD-0101 was labelled 4.81 against a computed 5.81, and RD-0109 was labelled
 220→below the autonomous cap when its real delta was above it. Both were fixed by correcting the label
 221→and the case, not the test.
 222→
 223→**The guard was then audited by mutation testing**, and it was narrower than it claimed. Six
 224→deliberate corruptions passed a green suite: editing a threshold in the policy's parameters table,
 225→flipping a label's category (which silently disabled every evidence check for that case), flipping
 226→a record's category, putting a non-zero amount on a no-action label, pre-committing an amount on an
 227→escalated label, and raising the runtime cap above the policy's. Each now has a test and each now
 228→fails. The lesson worth keeping: a guard is only as good as the last attempt to defeat it, and the
 229→comment in the test file claiming it caught policy-threshold drift was simply untrue until someone
 230→tried it.
 231→
 232→Every case also runs end to end through the real pipeline without error.
 233→
 234→### Evaluation
 235→
 236→Run `python3 -m app.eval` to evaluate every labelled case. Use `--pack NAME` repeatedly to select
 237→packs, `--llm mock|tencent` to choose the provider, and `--out DIR` to choose the output root.
 238→Reports land under `<out>/<pack>/report.json` and `<out>/<pack>/report.md`, with case artifacts
 239→beside them. “Decisions matching the label” means outcome, action, and cent-rounded amount agree
 240→with the label. “Rulings citing every decisive rule” means every non-`ESC-` decisive label rule
 241→appears in the candidate's citations. Stopping to ask the party counts as a miss. A mock run
 242→checks wiring only; this section makes no score claim. A case the model could not answer is
 243→scored `model failed`, never a match, and makes the command exit 2.
 244→
 245→## Known limitations
 246→
 247→- **Seventeen cases is a demonstration corpus, not a benchmark.** It is sized to cover every rule
 248→  path and every outcome, not to support a statistically meaningful accuracy claim. Do not quote a
 249→  percentage from it without the denominator attached.
 250→- **No adversarial or ambiguous-language cases.** Every intake form is coherently written. Real
 251→  filings are terse, contradictory, and sometimes in Singlish. A system tuned on this corpus will
 252→  look better than it is on real text.
 253→- **Chat logs are short and clean.** The lexicon signals in the pack fire predictably here, which
 254→  makes them look more informative than GEN-9 says they are.
 255→- **One trip archetype.** All routes are generated from the same bearing-walk, so their geometry is
 256→  more uniform than a real fleet's.
 257→- **The labels are ours.** Where the policy is `[SYNTHESISED]`, the "correct" answer is a judgement
 258→  the team made. A Ryde operations reviewer might rule differently on RD-0104 or RD-0105, and that
 259→  disagreement would be about policy, not about the system.
 260→
 261→## If a real dataset arrives
 262→
 263→Drop it in as a new pack — `data/packs/<name>/` with `disputes/`, `ground-truth.json` and
 264→`pack.json` — in either record shape (both are documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`), then set
 265→`dataset_pack` in `app/config.json` or pass `--pack <name>`. Keep this corpus as the **held-out
 266→labelled set**: a real dataset supplied without ground-truth labels cannot measure accuracy, so the
 267→synthesised labelled corpus stays useful even when it is no longer the primary input.
 268→

Entry for the **Tencent Cloud "AI CAN DO IT" Hackathon Singapore 2026**, Digital Native track
(the Ryde challenge statement, section 5 of the organisers' document).

**Status: building (since 2026-09-21).** The scope
is ruled: a two-category MVP (route deviation + no-show charge) with three agents, a
deterministic evidence layer, and an observable case-file view. The challenge statement is in
[`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md); the builder's contract is in
[`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md).

## The challenge

Ride-hailing platforms process thousands of dispute tickets daily: fare disputes, route deviations,
property damage, safety incidents, no-show charges. They are subjective, emotionally charged, and
currently resolved by humans reviewing GPS telemetry, chat logs, payment records and company policy
by hand. The result is slow, expensive and inconsistent.

The task is an autonomous multi-agent system that gathers evidence, builds both sides' cases, applies
company policy and issues a fair ruling with a confidence score and a plain-language explanation.

## Architecture

Three core agents, all MVP-required:

| Agent | Role |
|---|---|
| **Rider Advocate** | Builds the rider's case from the Evidence Pack and the policy |
| **Driver Advocate** | Builds the driver's case from the Evidence Pack and the policy |
| **Judge** | Weighs both cases, applies policy, rules, and explains the reasoning with a confidence score |

Inter-agent communication must be **observable** — a judge needs to see how the agents exchange
information and build their cases. That surface is a required deliverable, not a nice-to-have.

The full walkthrough — components, lifecycle, gates, observability — is in
[`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md). The system on one page:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> B["Server"]
    PACK --> CL["Command-line runner"]
    A["Rider intake form"] --> B
    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
    CL --> C
    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
    POL --> J["Judge"]
    E --> RA
    E --> DA
    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
    DA --> S
    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
    S -- "No" --> J
    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
    O2 -- "Candidate ruling queued" --> H
    J -- "Model could not answer" --> H
    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
    J -.-> L
    L -- "Embedded in the case file" --> K["Operator console"]
```

## Documents

- [`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md) — the challenge statement, verbatim
- [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) — architecture diagram and system description
- [`docs/policy.md`](docs/policy.md) — the policy rule set the Judge applies, with per-rule provenance
- [`docs/dataset.md`](docs/dataset.md) — the labelled corpus, its provenance and its limitations
- [`docs/evidence-plan.md`](docs/evidence-plan.md) — development-process evidence rules
- [`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md) — builder's entry point and project memory

## Development tooling

Built with Tencent Cloud **CodeBuddy**. The competition mandates proof of product usage, so
development happens in the tool and evidence is captured as it occurs.

## Run

No dependencies and no API key needed for the skeleton: it runs on a stock Python 3.9+ with the
standard library only, using a deterministic mock in place of the LLM.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0101
python3 -m app.cli --pack organiser-style-v1 --dispute DISP-002
```

`--dispute` takes either a dispute id inside the selected pack or a path to a record file
(`python3 -m app.cli --dispute data/packs/ryde-synth-v1/disputes/RD-0101.json`). The pack
defaults to `dataset_pack` in `app/config.json`; `--pack` overrides it for one run.

That prints the agent-to-agent event strip and the ruling, and writes the run's artifacts to
`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).

The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
of the records the agents see.

Three gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **all three are enforced in Python, not
asked of the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold, ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap, and
ESC-2, which withholds a route-case ruling when the deviation cannot be measured. Try them:

```bash
python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0109   # withheld: above the cap
python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0108   # withheld: no deviation to measure
```

**Mock by default.** The default provider is a deterministic mock. Its free-text fields (claim
summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation) are prefixed `MOCK`; actions, amounts, rule IDs and
evidence refs are not. A mock run is a plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling. The real model is
Tencent Cloud ADP, one app per agent: put the three app keys in `.env` (see `.env.example`), then
run `python3 -m app.server --llm tencent` or `python3 -m app.cli --llm tencent --dispute <id>`.

The demo walkthrough and its recording land once the case-file UI and the real LLM call are in.

`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).

The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
of the records the agents see.

Three gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **all three are enforced in Python, not
asked of the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold, ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap, and
ESC-2, which withholds a route-case ruling when the deviation cannot be measured. Try them:

```bash
python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0109   # withheld: above the cap
python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0108   # withheld: no deviation to measure
```

**Mock by default.** The default provider is a deterministic mock. Its free-text fields (claim
summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation) are prefixed `MOCK`; actions, amounts, rule IDs and
evidence refs are not. A mock run is a plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling. The real model is
Tencent Cloud ADP, one app per agent: put the three app keys in `.env` (see `.env.example`), then
run `python3 -m app.server --llm tencent` or `python3 -m app.cli --llm tencent --dispute <id>`.

The demo walkthrough and its recording land once the case-file UI and the real LLM call are in.

def _is_figure(value: Any) -> bool:
    """True only for a real number. bool is an int subclass, so it is excluded."""

def _is_count(value: Any) -> bool:
    """True only for a real integer. bool is an int subclass, so it is excluded."""

def ns6_auto_refund_eligible(pack: EvidencePack) -> bool:
    """NS-6: whether a contested no-show refund may be issued without a human.

    Every condition must hold, and a missing figure always fails its condition: an
    unrecorded fee, fraud flag or dispute history is not a clean record. This decides
    who decides the case, never which way it goes.

    if cancellation is None:

    if not _is_count(total) or not _is_count(upheld):
        return False
    if total < 0 or upheld < 0 or upheld > total:

appears in the candidate's citations. Stopping to ask the party counts as a miss. A mock run
checks wiring only; this section makes no score claim. A case the model could not answer is
scored `model failed`, never a match, and makes the command exit 2.

## Known limitations

- **Seventeen cases is a demonstration corpus, not a benchmark.** It is sized to cover every rule
  path and every outcome, not to support a statistically meaningful accuracy claim. Do not quote a
  percentage from it without the denominator attached.
- **No adversarial or ambiguous-language cases.** Every intake form is coherently written. Real
  filings are terse, contradictory, and sometimes in Singlish. A system tuned on this corpus will
  look better than it is on real text.
- **Chat logs are short and clean.** The lexicon signals in the pack fire predictably here, which
  makes them look more informative than GEN-9 says they are.
- **One trip archetype.** All routes are generated from the same bearing-walk, so their geometry is
  more uniform than a real fleet's.
- **The labels are ours.** Where the policy is `[SYNTHESISED]`, the "correct" answer is a judgement
  the team made. A Ryde operations reviewer might rule differently on RD-0104 or RD-0105, and that
  disagreement would be about policy, not about the system.

## If a real dataset arrives

Drop it in as a new pack — `data/packs/<name>/` with `disputes/`, `ground-truth.json` and
`pack.json` — in either record shape (both are documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`), then set
`dataset_pack` in `app/config.json` or pass `--pack <name>`. Keep this corpus as the **held-out
labelled set**: a real dataset supplied without ground-truth labels cannot measure accuracy, so the
synthesised labelled corpus stays useful even when it is no longer the primary input.
'

## Known limitations

- **Seventeen cases is a demonstration corpus, not a benchmark.** It is sized to cover every rule
  path and every outcome, not to support a statistically meaningful accuracy claim. Do not quote a
  percentage from it without the denominator attached.
- **No adversarial or ambiguous-language cases.** Every intake form is coherently written. Real
  filings are terse, contradictory, and sometimes in Singlish. A system tuned on this corpus will
  look better than it is on real text.
- **Chat logs are short and clean.** The lexicon signals in the pack fire predictably here, which
  makes them look more informative than GEN-9 says they are.
- **One trip archetype.** All routes are generated from the same bearing-walk, so their geometry is
  more uniform than a real fleet's.
- **The labels are ours.** Where the policy is `[SYNTHESISED]`, the "correct" answer is a judgement
  the team made. A Ryde operations reviewer might rule differently on RD-0104 or RD-0105, and that
  disagreement would be about policy, not about the system.

## If a real dataset arrives

Drop it in as a new pack — `data/packs/<name>/` with `disputes/`, `ground-truth.json` and
`pack.json` — in either record shape (both are documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`), then set
`dataset_pack` in `app/config.json` or pass `--pack <name>`. Keep this corpus as the **held-out
labelled set**: a real dataset supplied without ground-truth labels cannot measure accuracy, so the
synthesised labelled corpus stays useful even when it is no longer the primary input.
